paragraph.text: F13. "Vegan restaurants also call the exterminator and kill insects"

it's true that vegan restaurants, like any food business, carry out pest control, and that local councils spray insecticide in parks, schools and streets. Many vegans face this at home too: the building's body corporate sprays the common areas, the lease asks for the property to be treated, termites attack the timber. But a restaurant doesn't get to choose whether to control pests: food-safety rules require every food business to keep the premises free of cockroaches, rats and flies, and Brazil's own rule says to prevent first and use chemical control only when prevention doesn't work. Pest control responds to a real conflict with animals who contaminate food; raising animals to eat brings billions of victims into existence with no conflict at all. Public spraying and the spraying of a building are decided by the authorities or by the owners' meeting, not by each resident. And those who eat meat escape none of this: animal farming also uses insecticides, in poultry sheds, for example. The consistent path is to demand the methods that kill the fewest, not to give up on sparing those who can be spared.
killing mosquitoes, rats and cockroaches yourself is covered in F6; this chapter is about pest control carried out by companies, in restaurants, apartment buildings, rented homes and public places

"That vegan restaurant gets the exterminator in every month. And the council sprays poison in the park and you don't say a word. In your building, the body corporate sprays the car park and you pay the levy. So you kill animals too."
Vegan restaurants carry out pest control, and the buildings and houses vegans live in are sprayed too, which kills insects and rodents.
Vegans eat at and support these restaurants, and they pay the taxes that fund the spraying of public places.
If veganism were consistent, vegans would refuse everything that kills animals.
So vegans also accept killing animals when it's convenient, and can't condemn those who eat meat.

P1 is true. P2 is true, but opening a restaurant, living in an apartment building or living in a city isn't choosing to kill insects: pest control is required by law of every food business, vegan or not, and spraying a building is decided collectively. P3 confuses veganism with a promise never to cause any death; the most widely used definition talks about avoiding exploitation and cruelty "as far as is possible and practicable". And the conclusion doesn't follow: even if a vegan fell short here, that wouldn't make raising and slaughtering animals acceptable.
fails at P3, which demands a purity veganism doesn't promise, and in the leap to the conclusion, which turns a possible inconsistency into permission to cause more harm.

Every kitchen that cooks for lots of people has to stay clean and free of cockroaches, rats and flies, because they can make people sick. That's true of every restaurant, vegan or not, and of the buildings we live in too. But there are ways to keep these animals away without killing them: closing up the holes, keeping food in sealed containers, taking the rubbish out every day. Poison is only for when none of that works. That's very different from raising a chicken just to eat her later: the chicken wasn't bothering anyone.

Every restaurant, vegan or not, is required by law to keep its kitchen free of cockroaches, rats and flies, because they contaminate food. And Brazil's own rule says to prevent first and use poison only when prevention isn't enough. That's a real conflict with animals who threaten health, and it isn't the same as raising animals to eat. Spraying parks and schools is decided by the council, and spraying the building by the body corporate; what a vegan can do, at home and in the city, is push for prevention and methods that kill fewer. And those who eat meat don't escape it: animal farming also uses insecticides, in poultry sheds, for example. If these deaths can be reduced, the way is to demand methods that kill fewer, not to kill more.
"If the vegan restaurant calls the exterminator, and so does the one serving chicken, what changes when you choose the chicken?"

text.bold: 1. A restaurant doesn't choose whether to control pests.

paragraph.text: In Brazil, ANVISA's resolution RDC 216/2004 requires every food service to keep its premises free of vectors and urban pests, with ongoing prevention. In Australia, Standard 3.2.2 of the Food Standards Code requires a business to do everything it reasonably can to prevent pest problems. This applies to every restaurant, vegan or not, just as it applies to hospitals, schools and supermarkets.

text.bold: 2. The rule itself puts poison last.

paragraph.text: RDC 216 says chemical control should be used when prevention measures aren't effective, and carried out by a specialized company. It's the same order defended in F6: prevent first, then use the least harmful means, and kill only as a last resort. Integrated pest management, recommended by agencies such as the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), follows the same logic: monitor, prevent, and apply products only when needed, leaving broadcast spraying as a last resort.

Cockroaches, rats and flies in a kitchen threaten the health of the people who eat there. That's different from bringing billions of animals into existence each year in order to kill them. Veganism is about avoidable exploitation and cruelty, "as far as is possible and practicable", and doesn't promise that no one will ever cause an animal's death.

text.bold: 4. Public spraying isn't the taxpayer's choice.

paragraph.text: Whoever decides to spray insecticide in a park or send out the fogging truck is the authorities. A vegan can, like any citizen, push for better methods, but can't stop paying tax or single-handedly prevent the spraying. Blaming each taxpayer for every government decision would also mean blaming meat-eaters for each one of them.

text.bold: 5. At home, vegans often don't decide alone.

paragraph.text: People who live in an apartment building pay the levy for spraying decided by the building manager or at the owners' meeting; renters may have to hand the property back treated, if the lease asks for it. What can be done is to propose alternatives: sealing gaps and drains, keeping common areas and bins clean, hiring companies that work with integrated pest management and apply products only where there are pests, not as routine. With termites, which can damage the timber and structure of a house, the conflict is real, and the order is the same as in F6: prevent (control moisture, keep timber off the soil, inspect), treat only where there's an infestation, and choose the method that causes the least harm.

text.bold: 6. Prevention protects more, in public places too.

paragraph.text: Against dengue, fogging kills only the adult mosquitoes it reaches and is reserved for outbreaks; the main measure is removing breeding sites. The

method, which doesn't kill off mosquito populations, cut dengue by 77% in a randomized trial in Indonesia and was associated with 69% fewer cases in Niterói, Brazil. Demanding these methods is what a consistent animal advocate does.

text.bold: 7. Those who eat meat escape none of this.

paragraph.text: The restaurant serving chicken also has its kitchen treated. And animal farming has its own pest control: in poultry sheds, the lesser mealworm (

), a beetle that spreads through the birds' litter, is fought with insecticides and mechanical methods. Choosing meat doesn't reduce insect deaths in the slightest; it only adds the deaths of the animals raised.
If some vegan or vegan restaurant used poison without need, that would be their failure, not a licence to raise and slaughter animals. It's the tu quoque fallacy (L11).

There's a realistic possibility that insects are sentient (A3). So the answer shouldn't be "insects don't count", but "we can kill fewer": vegan restaurants can prefer companies that work with integrated management, sealing and monitoring, and the movement can demand the same of the authorities.

(d) The strongest counter-reply: nobody has to open a restaurant

The most serious version says that opening a restaurant is a choice. Whoever opens one knows they'll need to kill insects and rats, and opens it anyway, for profit. So the vegan restaurant owner accepts killing animals for an economic interest, the same kind of interest that drives animal farming.
(e) Why the reply doesn't reach the conclusion

text.bold: A vegan restaurant is good for society, and for animals.

paragraph.text: Every dish served there replaces a meal that, in another restaurant, would have had meat, dairy or eggs. Vegan restaurants show that food without animal products is tasty and doable, welcome people who are starting to change, and help many people cut back. People will keep eating out; if there's no vegan restaurant, they'll eat where animals are served, and where pest control happens too. Not opening the restaurant wouldn't spare any cockroaches; it would only spare fewer animals.

Kitchens, markets, warehouses, vegetable gardens and farms all have to deal with them, and every society needs places that make food. What's at stake isn't whether there's any pest control, but how much harm it causes.

In a restaurant, a cockroach's death is a side effect that can be reduced with sealing and cleaning; if no cockroach shows up, all the better. In animal farming, the animal's death is the product itself.

Pest control doesn't exist to make a profit, but to protect the health of the people who eat there, a serious interest. In animal farming, the animal is killed to satisfy a taste that can be satisfied in other ways (J6).
If the criticism is that the restaurant could kill fewer, it's welcome: the way is to demand better methods, not to give up on caring about animals.

The principle being tested is: "if you take part in something that kills animals, you lose the right to criticize any other way of killing animals".
Anyone who uses a hospital that sprays for pests couldn't criticize cruelty to dogs
Anyone who pays tax couldn't criticize any public policy
They couldn't criticize cockfighting or elephant hunting either, because their restaurant sprays
Anyone who drives and has hit an insect couldn't support speed limits

The argument points to something real: vegan restaurants, like all others, kill insects and rodents, and public spraying kills many animals, including ones who threaten no one. Animal advocates shouldn't pretend this doesn't count. It's also true that not all pest control follows the order the rule itself sets: there's routine spraying with no need.

But the consistent response is to demand prevention and methods that kill fewer, from the restaurant and from the council, not to conclude that it makes no difference. Pest control responds to a real conflict; raising animals to eat is a choice that can be avoided.
